The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) inherited from the finite
coherent-resolution and cohomological suppliers. Let $k$ be a field and let $X$
be a smooth equidimensional $k$-scheme of finite type
([[def-smooth-morphism-schemes]]), with Chow ring $A^*(X)$
([[thm-intersection-product-and-chow-ring-of-a-smooth-scheme]]) and
vector-bundle group $K^0(X)$
([[def-grothendieck-group-of-coherent-sheaves-and-vector-bundles-on-a-scheme]]).
When $X$ is additionally quasi-projective,
[[lem-k-zero-vector-bundles-versus-coherent-sheaves]] identifies this group with
coherent $K_0(X)$; that extra hypothesis is required for the coherent-group
extension. Write $A^*(X)_{\mathbb Q}:=A^*(X)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$. If $n=\dim X$,
$A^i(X)=A_{n-i}(X)=0$ for $i>n$, since there are no negative-dimensional
integral cycles. Every series below is evaluated only through degree $n$;
in particular positive-codimension elements are nilpotent. For the rank-zero
bundle the empty root list gives $\operatorname{ch}(0)=0$ and
$\operatorname{td}(0)=1$.

**Chern roots.** The **Chern roots** of a finite locally free
$\mathcal O_X$-module $\mathcal E$ of rank $r$ are formal symbols
$x_1,\dots,x_r$ with the property that the elementary symmetric functions in the
$x_i$ are the Chern classes: $e_i(x_1,\dots,x_r)=c_i(\mathcal E)$
([[def-chern-classes-of-a-vector-bundle]]); by the splitting principle every
symmetric polynomial expression in the $x_i$ with rational coefficients defines
a well-defined element of $A^*(X)_{\mathbb Q}$
([[lem-chern-class-naturality-additivity-and-splitting]]).

**Chern character.** Define
$$\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal E):=\sum_{j=1}^{r}e^{x_j}=\sum_{m\ge0}\frac{1}{m!}\,p_m(c_1,\dots,c_m)\in A^*(X)_{\mathbb Q},$$
where $p_0:=r=\operatorname{rank}\mathcal E$, while for $m\ge1$ the
power sum $p_m(c_1,\dots,c_m)=\sum_jx_j^m$ is a universal polynomial in
the Chern classes. Thus $\operatorname{ch}_0(\mathcal E)=r$; explicitly
$\operatorname{ch}=r+c_1+\tfrac12(c_1^2-2c_2)+\tfrac16(c_1^3-3c_1c_2+3c_3)+\cdots$
(the denominators are why we tensor with $\mathbb Q$).

**Todd class.** Define
$$\operatorname{td}(\mathcal E):=\prod_{j=1}^{r}\frac{x_j}{1-e^{-x_j}}\in A^*(X)_{\mathbb Q};$$
explicitly
$\operatorname{td}(\mathcal E)=1+\tfrac12c_1+\tfrac1{12}(c_1^2+c_2)+\tfrac1{24}c_1c_2+\cdots$.
For a smooth $X$ the **Todd class of $X$** is $\operatorname{td}(T_X)$ for the
tangent bundle $T_X=\operatorname{Hom}(\Omega^1_{X/k},\mathcal O_X)$
([[def-sheaf-relative-differentials]],
[[thm-differentials-smooth-locally-free]]).

**Line bundles.** For an invertible sheaf $\mathcal L$ with
$x=c_1(\mathcal L)$: $\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal L)=e^{x}$ and
$\operatorname{td}(\mathcal L)=x/(1-e^{-x})=1+\tfrac12x+\tfrac1{12}x^2-\cdots$.

**Well-definedness.** After truncation at degree $n$, the positive-degree
components of the Chern character and all components of the Todd class are
symmetric polynomials with rational coefficients in the Chern roots, hence
universal polynomial expressions in their elementary symmetric functions,
the Chern classes of [[def-chern-classes-of-a-vector-bundle]]. The degree-zero
component of the Chern character is the rank $r$. Thus the Chern character
depends only on the rank and Chern classes of $\mathcal E$, whereas the Todd
class depends only on its Chern classes. For locally constant ranks these
formulas are interpreted componentwise on the finite open-and-closed rank
loci. By the splitting principle of
[[lem-chern-class-naturality-additivity-and-splitting]], these values are
independent of the choice of flag bundle or filtration: any two filtrations
have the same rank and elementary symmetric functions, and hence give the
same polynomial values. Rational coefficients are needed for
the exponential and geometric expansions, which is why the target is
$A^*(X)\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$. The tangent bundle is finite locally free
of rank $\dim X$ by [[thm-differentials-smooth-locally-free]], so its Chern
roots and Todd class are defined; the Todd class is multiplicative in exact sequences, whereas the Chern
character is additive, and the
identification of $K^0(X)$ with $K_0(X)$ on a quasi-projective $X$ lets the
character be evaluated on coherent classes through the finite locally free
resolutions of [[lem-k-zero-vector-bundles-versus-coherent-sheaves]].

Assume AC. For every $N\geq0$ identify
$\mathbb{CP}^N=\operatorname{Gr}_1(\mathbb C^{N+1})$, the space of complex
lines in $\mathbb C^{N+1}$, and let $\gamma$ be the tautological complex line
with $x=e(\gamma_{\mathbb R})\in H^2(\mathbb{CP}^N;\mathbb Z)$ its Euler class
in the complex orientation. Then, as a graded ring,
$$H^*(\mathbb{CP}^N;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[x]/(x^{N+1}),$$
the class $x$ generating each even degree and the odd groups vanishing; for
$0\leq m\leq N$ the standard inclusion
$\mathbb{CP}^m\hookrightarrow\mathbb{CP}^N$, induced by
$\mathbb C^{m+1}\subseteq\mathbb C^{N+1}$, pulls $x$ back to $x$.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a closed $R$-oriented smooth $n$-manifold, where $R=\mathbb Z$ or $\mathbb F_2$, and let $Z\subseteq M$ be a closed $R$-oriented embedded $z$-submanifold. Put $r=n-z$ and orient $
u_Z=TM|_Z/TZ$ in tangent-first order: $\det TM|_Z=\det TZ\otimes\det
u_Z$. Choose a smooth metric and a tubular chart whose differential induces the identity on this normal quotient; restrict to a sufficiently small closed disk bundle. Such normalized charts exist by the construction in [[thm-tubular-neighbourhood-theorem-in-a-smooth-ambient-manifold]].

The normalized Thom class $u_
u\in H^r(D(
u),S(
u);R)$ corresponds to a class $\alpha\in H^r(M,M\setminus Z;R)$ by the punctured-fibre comparison and tubular excision. Write $ ar\alpha\in H^r(M;R)$ for its relative-to-absolute image. Then
$$ ar\alpha\cap[M]=(-1)^{rz}(i_Z)_*[Z]\in H_z(M;R).$$
Equivalently, $ ar\alpha=(-1)^{rz}D_M^{-1}((i_Z)_*[Z])$. The sign is the shuffle from tangent-first coordinates to normal-first cap evaluation. Over $\mathbb F_2$ all orientations are canonical and the sign disappears. A relative class capped directly with the absolute $[M]$ instead has relative homology as target; the displayed formula uses $ ar\alpha$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a commutative
ring with $1$ ([[def-commutative-ring]]), let $n\ge0$, let $d\in\mathbb Z$ and
let $X=\mathbb P^n_A\cong\operatorname{Proj}A[x_0,\dots,x_n]$ be relative
projective space ([[def-relative-projective-space-standard-charts]],
[[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]]), with twisting sheaf
$\mathcal O_X(d)$ ([[def-twisting-sheaf-proj]]) and cohomology
$H^q(X,\mathcal O_X(d))$. Then
$$H^q(X,\mathcal O_X(d))=0\qquad\text{unless }q=0\text{ or }q=n.$$
If $n>0$, then $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(d))\cong A[x_0,\dots,x_n]_d$ when $d\ge0$
and $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(d))=0$ when $d<0$, where
$A[x_0,\dots,x_n]_d$ is the degree-$d$ graded piece
([[def-graded-ring-and-graded-module]]); and $H^n(X,\mathcal O_X(d))$ is the
free $A$-module on the Laurent monomials $x_0^{e_0}\cdots x_n^{e_n}$ with
$e_i<0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_ie_i=d$, so that it is nonzero precisely when
$d\le-n-1$ and $A\ne0$. For $n=0$ one has $\mathbb P^0_A=\operatorname{Spec}A$
and $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(d))\cong A$ for every $d\in\mathbb Z$, with all higher
groups zero. The zero ring $A=0$ is allowed: then $X=\varnothing$ and all
groups are zero, in agreement with both displayed descriptions.

second-countable smooth manifold, possibly with boundary or empty, and let
$\rho_M:H^*(M;\mathbb Z)\to H^*(M;\mathbb R)$ be induced by
$\mathbb Z\hookrightarrow\mathbb R$. Write $J_M$ for the natural de Rham
isomorphism from real de Rham cohomology to singular cohomology with real
coefficients.

For every finite-rank smooth complex bundle $E\to M$ with a Hermitian metric
and Hermitian connection $\nabla$, and every $j\geq0$,
$$J_M([c_j(\nabla)])=\rho_M(c_j(E)).$$
For every finite-rank smooth real bundle $V\to M$ with any real connection
$D$, and every $j\geq0$,
$$J_M([p_j(D)])=\rho_M(p_j(V)).$$
For every oriented Euclidean bundle $W\to M$ of even rank with a
metric-compatible connection $\nabla$, and its Thom-normalized Euler class,
$$J_M([e(\nabla)])=\rho_M(e(W)).$$
Here $c_j(\nabla)$, $p_j(D)$, and $e(\nabla)$ use the normalizations in
[[def-chern-pontryagin-and-euler-characteristic-forms]], while $c_j(E)$,
$p_j(V)$, and $e(W)$ are the published topological classes. In particular
$c_1(L)=e(L_{\mathbb R})$ for a complex line and
$p_j(V)=(-1)^j c_{2j}(V_{\mathbb C})$. These are equalities after passage to
real coefficients; no equality with integral torsion is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) inherited from the
smooth-immersion and homological suppliers. Let $k$ be a field, $X$ a smooth
equidimensional $k$-scheme of finite type, and let
$0\to\mathcal E'\to\mathcal E\to\mathcal E''\to0$ be a short exact sequence of
finite locally free $\mathcal O_X$-modules
([[def-locally-free-sheaf-finite-rank]]). Ranks are allowed to be locally
constant: define Chern classes componentwise on the finitely many open-and-closed
rank loci, using [[def-chern-classes-of-a-vector-bundle]] on each constant-rank locus. Then:

1. (Whitney additivity) $c(\mathcal E)=c(\mathcal E')\,c(\mathcal E'')$ in the
   Chow ring $A^*(X)$ ([[def-chern-classes-of-a-vector-bundle]],
   [[thm-intersection-product-and-chow-ring-of-a-smooth-scheme]]).
2. (Naturality) If $f:X'\to X$ is a flat morphism of smooth equidimensional
   $k$-schemes of finite type, then $c_i(f^*\mathcal E)=f^*c_i(\mathcal E)$ for all $i$.
3. (Splitting principle) There exists a morphism $f:X'\to X$, a composition of
   projective bundles over $X$, with $X'$ smooth and equidimensional, such that
   $f^*:A^*(X)\to A^*(X')$ is injective. On each rank locus
   $X_r=\{x:\operatorname{rank}_x\mathcal E=r\}$, its inverse image admits a filtration
   $$0=\mathcal E_0\subseteq\mathcal E_1\subseteq\dots\subseteq\mathcal E_r=f^*\mathcal E$$
   with successive quotients invertible sheaves
   $\mathcal L_1,\dots,\mathcal L_r$; consequently
   $f^*c(\mathcal E)=\prod_{i=1}^r(1+c_1(\mathcal L_i))$. Any polynomial identity
   among Chern classes that is proved on every rank locus after replacing $\mathcal E$ by such a
   filtered bundle and $c_i(\mathcal E)$ by the elementary symmetric functions
   $e_i(c_1(\mathcal L_j))$ holds for $\mathcal E$ itself.
4. (Consequences) $c_i(\mathcal E^\vee)=(-1)^ic_i(\mathcal E)$;
   $c_1(\mathcal L\otimes\mathcal M)=c_1(\mathcal L)+c_1(\mathcal M)$ for
   invertible sheaves; $c_i(\mathcal E)=0$ for
   $i>r$ on $X_r$; and for an exact sequence of vector
   bundles the total Chern classes multiply (this is (1)).

Exactness gives $0\to K\to\mathcal O^{2k+N}\to\mathcal O(1)^k\to0$ and $0\to\mathcal O(-1)^k\to K\to\mathcal F\to0$. By [F7], additivity of the Chern character in these short exact sequences gives
$$
\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal F)=(2k+N)\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal O)-k\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal O(-1))-k\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal O(1)).
$$
By [F4], the cohomology groups of $\mathcal O(-1)$, $\mathcal O$, and $\mathcal O(1)$ are finite-dimensional and vanish above degree three. The long exact sequences [F8] then give the same finiteness and vanishing for $K$ and $\mathcal F$, so [F8] also gives additivity of $\chi$. Since $\chi(\mathcal O(-1))=0$, $\chi(\mathcal O)=1$, and $\chi(\mathcal O(1))=4$ by [F4], we obtain $\chi(\mathcal F)=(2k+N)-4k-0=N-2k$.

The quaternionic coordinates in the Statement give local product charts for $\pi$: on the finite chart, with $v=\lambda_2/\lambda_1$, the base coordinates $z_1,z_2$ recover the remaining affine coordinates by $\mu_1/\lambda_1=z_1-\bar z_2v$ and $\mu_2/\lambda_1=z_2+\bar z_1v$; the charts with $\lambda_2\ne0$ and the reciprocal quaternionic chart at infinity cover the omitted points. Hence $\pi$ is a smooth submersion, and each fiber $L_x=\pi^{-1}(x)$ is a closed complex linear $\mathbb P^1\subset\mathbb P^3$. Let $\omega_x\in H^4(S^4,S^4\setminus\{x\};\mathbb Z)$ be the positive local orientation class, whose image in absolute cohomology is $u$. In a local product chart over an oriented ball around $x$, the pulled-back relative class $\pi^*\omega_x$ is the positive generator on every normal four-disk to $L_x$; it is therefore the normalized Thom class of that fiber, with normal orientation induced from the oriented base. Its absolute image is $\pi^*u$. The fiber has real dimension $2$ and codimension $4$, so [F3] gives the sign $(-1)^{4\cdot2}=+1$ and identifies $\pi^*u$ with the Poincaré dual of $[L_x]$. To identify this dual class, choose two complex hyperplanes meeting transversely in $L_x$. Their positive normal Thom classes multiply to the positive normal Thom class of $L_x$ (in local holomorphic coordinates this is the product of the two complex-disk generators); by [F6] each hyperplane class is $H_{\rm top}$. Thus the Poincaré dual of $[L_x]$ is $H_{\rm top}^2$, proving $\pi^*u=H_{\rm top}^2$.

In the algebraic Chow ring, [F1] and $H=c_1(\mathcal O(1))$ give
$$
\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal F)=(2k+N)-ke^{-H}-ke^H=N-kH^2,
$$
because $H^4=0$ on the complex threefold and the odd powers cancel. The integral Whitney formula [F7] applied to the same two sequences gives $c^{\rm alg}(\mathcal F)=(1-H^2)^{-k}=1+kH^2$ through codimension three, so $c_1^{\rm alg}(\mathcal F)=0$ and $c_2^{\rm alg}(\mathcal F)=kH^2$ integrally. In the underlying topological category the same exact sequences are exact sequences of complex vector bundles, so [F5] and the line-class identity $c_1(\mathcal O(1))=H$ give
$$
c(\mathcal F)=\frac{1}{(1-H)^k(1+H)^k}=(1-H^2)^{-k}=1+kH^2
$$
through degree six, since $H^4=0$. Hence the topological classes are $c_1(\mathcal F)=0$, $c_2(\mathcal F)=kH^2$, and $c_3(\mathcal F)=0$. The universal formulas $\operatorname{ch}_1=c_1$, $\operatorname{ch}_2=\tfrac12(c_1^2-2c_2)$, and $\operatorname{ch}_3=\tfrac16(c_1^3-3c_1c_2+3c_3)$ then give the topological $\operatorname{ch}(\mathcal F)=N-kH^2$. This compares only the identical finite line-bundle resolution and its line class, not arbitrary analytic and algebraic cohomology.

Write $c_2(E)=m u$ for $m\in\mathbb Z$. Naturality of Chern classes and the pullback hypothesis give $mH^2=\pi^*c_2(E)=c_2(\mathcal F)=kH^2$ by steps 2.1 and 1.2. Since $H^2$ is a nonzero generator by [F2], $m=k$, proving both the stated Chern class and its evaluation on $[S^4]$.

For an integer $n\ge1$, **complex projective space** is the set of complex lines in $\mathbb C^{n+1}$ with the quotient topology
$$\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C):=(\mathbb C^{n+1}\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb C^\times,\qquad [z_0:\cdots:z_n]:=\mathbb C^\times(z_0,\ldots,z_n).$$
The quotient projection is continuous and surjective. Its restriction to the unit sphere $S^{2n+1}\subset\mathbb C^{n+1}$ is still surjective, so $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ is compact. It is Hausdorff: the map sending a nonzero vector $z$ to the orthogonal projection $zz^*/\lVert z\rVert^2$ is continuous and constant on each complex line, hence descends by the quotient topology to a continuous injection from $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ into the Hausdorff space of complex matrices. A continuous injection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism onto its image.

For open $V\subseteq\mathbb C^r$, a map $H:V\to\mathbb C^s$ is **holomorphic** if at every $a\in V$ there is a complex-linear map $A_a:\mathbb C^r\to\mathbb C^s$ such that $H(a+h)=H(a)+A_a h+R_a(h)$ with $\lVert R_a(h)\rVert/\lVert h\rVert\to0$ as $h\to0$, $h\ne0$. When $r=1$, this is equivalent to each component being holomorphic in the sense of [[def-complex-differentiability-holomorphic-and-entire]], since a finite vector of scalar difference quotients converges exactly when each component does. A complex atlas consists of charts into $\mathbb C^n$ with holomorphic transitions in both directions.

For $j\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$ let $U_j:=\{[z_0:\cdots:z_n]:z_j\ne0\}$. These open sets cover projective space: their inverse images under the quotient projection are the open saturated sets where $z_j\ne0$. The **standard chart** is
$$\varphi_j:U_j\longrightarrow\mathbb C^n,\qquad [z_0:\cdots:z_n]\longmapsto (z_0/z_j,\ldots,\widehat{z_j/z_j},\ldots,z_n/z_j),$$
where the $j$th coordinate is omitted. It is well defined under rescaling. The coordinate-ratio map on the inverse image of $U_j$ is continuous and constant on each quotient fibre, so the quotient topology makes $\varphi_j$ continuous; its inverse inserts $1$ in the $j$th position and is continuous by composition with the quotient projection. Hence it is a homeomorphism. On $U_j\cap U_k$ the transition from the $j$th chart to the $k$th chart sends each coordinate $w_\ell=z_\ell/z_j$ ($\ell\ne j$) to $w_\ell/w_k$ for $\ell\ne k$, with the omitted $j$th coordinate equal to $1/w_k$. To check holomorphy at $a$ with $a_k\ne0$, set $a_j=1$ and $h_j=0$ for the omitted source coordinate. Each target coordinate has the expansion $(a_\ell+h_\ell)/(a_k+h_k)=a_\ell/a_k+h_\ell/a_k-a_\ell h_k/a_k^2+O(\lVert h\rVert^2)$ for $\ell\ne k$. The linear term is complex-linear, and the remainder estimate follows by expanding the reciprocal at the nonzero $a_k$. The inverse transition has the same form, so both are holomorphic. Thus these charts make $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ a complex manifold of complex dimension $n$ and a topological manifold of real dimension $2n$ in the sense of [[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]. The finite chart cover by second-countable copies of $\mathbb C^n$ gives a countable base. Its rational transition functions have smooth real coordinate expressions on their domains, so the atlas also defines the smooth structure in the sense of [[def-smooth-manifold]]. The space is path-connected: distinct lines represented by $u,v$ give the path $t\mapsto[(1-t)u+tv]$, whose vector never vanishes because $u,v$ are linearly independent; equal lines give a constant path. In particular, $\mathbb P^1(\mathbb C)$ is a Riemann surface in the sense of [[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]].

A map $F:X\to\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ from a Riemann surface is **holomorphic** when it is continuous and every component of each chart expression $\varphi_j\circ F$, written in a local coordinate of $X$, is holomorphic on the open set $F^{-1}(U_j)$. On an overlap, the new components are $f_\ell/f_k$ and $1/f_k$, where the $f_\ell$ are the old components and $f_k\ne0$. The scalar quotient rule gives their holomorphy ([[thm-algebra-of-complex-derivatives]]), so it suffices to check one target chart locally. Changing the source coordinate composes each scalar component with a one-variable holomorphic chart transition, where [[thm-chain-rule-for-complex-derivatives]] applies ([[def-holomorphic-and-meromorphic-map-of-riemann-surfaces]]). A **projective line** is the image in $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$ of a two-dimensional complex subspace of $\mathbb C^{n+1}$. Every invertible linear map of $\mathbb C^{n+1}$ induces a holomorphic projective linear transformation: in source and target standard charts its coordinates are ratios of affine-linear functions with nonzero denominator, and the same reciprocal expansion gives a complex-linear derivative; these transformations act transitively on $\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)$.

For $r\ge1$, let $\mathbb P^r(\mathbb C)$ be the set of complex lines in
$\mathbb C^{r+1}$, with its quotient complex-manifold structure, and write
$[Z_0:\cdots:Z_r]$ for the line through a nonzero vector
$(Z_0,\ldots,Z_r)$. For $i\in\{0,\ldots,r\}$ set
$U_i=\{[Z_0:\cdots:Z_r]:Z_i\ne0\}$; its standard coordinates are the ratios
$Z_j/Z_i$ for $j\ne i$. For each integer $k$, the **projective twisting line
bundle** $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(k)$ is obtained by gluing the trivial
holomorphic line bundles $U_i\times\mathbb C$ with local frames $e_i^{(k)}$
and transition rule
$$e_j^{(k)}=\left(\frac{Z_j}{Z_i}\right)^k e_i^{(k)}\quad\text{on }U_i\cap U_j.$$
The transition factors are holomorphic and nowhere zero on the overlaps, with
$g_{ii}=1$, $g_{ij}=g_{ji}^{-1}$, and $g_{ij}g_{j\ell}=g_{i\ell}$ on every
triple overlap; hence they define a holomorphic line bundle. The sheaf
$\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(k)$ assigns to an open set the holomorphic sections of
this bundle, and $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}:=\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(0)$ is the
structure sheaf.

On a chart $Z_j\ne0$ with $j\ne0$, put $w=Z_0/Z_j$. In local frames of
$\mathcal O(m-1)$ and $\mathcal O(m)$, multiplication by $Z_0$ is
multiplication by $w$ up to the invertible frame factor. The holomorphic
local ring has no zero divisors, so this map is injective on stalks. The
quotient map is restriction to $w=0$. If a holomorphic germ $f(u,w)$
restricts to zero there, then $f(u,0)=0$ and
$$f(u,w)=w\,g(u,w),\qquad g(u,w)=\int_0^1\frac{\partial f}{\partial w}(u,tw)\,dt.$$
On a sufficiently small polydisc the integrand is holomorphic in $(u,w)$;
its locally uniformly convergent power series may be integrated termwise,
so $g$ is holomorphic and the germ lies in $(w)$. Thus the kernel of
restriction is precisely the image of multiplication. On a chart not
meeting $H$, the section $Z_0$ is nowhere zero, so multiplication is an
isomorphism and the quotient sheaf is zero. These stalk calculations prove
exactness of the first sequence for every $m$.

Tensor the exact $m=0$ sequence by the locally free line bundle
$\mathcal O(-1)$. Tensoring is exact because on each stalk this bundle is a
free rank-one module. By the transition rule in [F2], its restriction to
$H$ is $\mathcal O_H(-1)$; hence
$i_*\mathcal O_H\otimes\mathcal O(-1)\cong i_*\mathcal O_H(-1)$ on each
stalk. The resulting exact sequence is
$$0\to\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(-2)\to\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(-1) \to i_*\mathcal O_H(-1)\to0,$$
as claimed.

Fix integers $N\ge1$ and $k\ge0$ and equip $V=\mathbb C^k$ and $W=\mathbb C^N$ with the standard Hermitian inner products $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_j\overline{u_j}v_j$, which are conjugate-linear in the first variable. For a linear map $T:E\to F$ between these spaces, its Hermitian adjoint $T^\dagger:F\to E$ is characterized by $\langle Tu,v\rangle_F=\langle u,T^\dagger v\rangle_E$; in the standard bases its matrix is the conjugate transpose. For $A,B\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$, define their commutator by $[A,B]:=AB-BA$. Let

$$\mathscr D_{k,N}=\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)^2\times\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(W,V)\times\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(V,W),\qquad \operatorname{Herm}(V)=\{H\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V):H^\dagger=H\}.$$

Here $\operatorname{Herm}(V)$ is regarded as a real vector space. A framed ADHM linear datum is $x=(B_1,B_2,I,J)\in\mathscr D_{k,N}$. The complex and real moment maps are the maps $\mu_{\mathbb C}:\mathscr D_{k,N}\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ and $\mu_{\mathbb R}:\mathscr D_{k,N}\to\operatorname{Herm}(V)$ defined by

$$\mu_{\mathbb C}(x)=[B_1,B_2]+IJ,\qquad \mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J.$$

The datum is stable if the vectors $B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(w)$, with $m\ge0$, $i_j\in\{1,2\}$ and $w\in W$, span $V$. It is costable if there is no nonzero subspace of $V$ invariant under both $B_i$ and contained in $\ker J$. It is regular if it is stable and costable. The group $GL(V)$ acts by $g\cdot x=(gB_1g^{-1},gB_2g^{-1},gI,Jg^{-1})$. Its unitary subgroup is $U(V)$.

Write $X^s=\{x:\mu_{\mathbb C}(x)=0,\ x\text{ stable}\}$, $X^{\mathrm{reg}}=\{x\in X^s:x\text{ costable}\}$ and, for real $\zeta\ge0$, $X_\zeta^U=\{x\in X^s:\mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=\zeta I_V\}$. Denote the corresponding orbit sets by $X^s/GL(V)$, $X^{\mathrm{reg}}/GL(V)$ and $X_\zeta^U/U(V)$, with quotient topologies when discussing their analytic spaces. A word frame consists of $k$ columns obtained by fixed words in $B_1,B_2$ applied to fixed standard basis vectors of $W$.

For $T_{\mathbb C}=(\mathbb C^*)^2\times(\mathbb C^*)^N$, write $t_1,t_2,e_1,\ldots,e_N$ for the coordinate characters and put $h=\operatorname{diag}(e_1^{-1},\ldots,e_N^{-1})$. Its action is $(t_1,t_2,h)\cdot x=(t_1B_1,t_2B_2,Ih^{-1},t_1t_2hJ)$. The compact torus is its subgroup on which all characters have modulus one. The framing representation thus has character $\sum_\alpha e_\alpha^{-1}$ and its dual has character $\sum_\alpha e_\alpha$.

These are finite-dimensional matrix definitions. They do not assert a real/complex quotient correspondence, a sheaf or ASD identification, or a noncompact pushforward. In particular, positive-FI stability and zero-FI regularity are distinct conditions; neither an endpoint identification nor an ordinary ASD interpretation follows from this definition.
The field $\mathbb C$ is algebraically closed.

derivations.claim: The adjoint of $b_z^\dagger$ is the column $b_z=(-B_2^\dagger+\bar z_2,\ B_1^\dagger-\bar z_1,\ I^\dagger)^T$. A covector $v^\dagger$ annihilates the image of $b_z^\dagger$ exactly when $B_i^\dagger v=\bar z_i v$ and $I^\dagger v=0$, equivalently $v^\dagger B_i=z_i v^\dagger$ and $v^\dagger I=0$. Such a nonzero covector annihilates every word vector $B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(w)$, so stability implies surjectivity for every $z$. Conversely, if the word span $Q$ is proper, it is invariant under both $B_i$ and contains $I(W)$. The complex moment equation makes the induced pair on $V/Q$ commute, since $IJ(V)\subseteq I(W)\subseteq Q$. By [F2] its dual has a common eigenvector; pulling that covector back to $V^*$ gives $v^\dagger I=0$ and $v^\dagger B_i=z_i v^\dagger$ for some $z$, so $b_z^\dagger$ is not surjective.

A nonzero vector in $\ker a_z$ is a common eigenvector of $B_1,B_2$ contained in $\ker J$, so costability implies injectivity for every $z$. Conversely, if a nonzero common invariant subspace $Q\subseteq\ker J$ exists, then $IJ(Q)=0$ and the complex moment equation gives $[B_1,B_2]|_Q=0$. The restrictions commute and have a common eigenvector by [F2]; this vector lies in $\ker a_z$ for its eigenvalues $z_1,z_2$. Thus the two affine rank criteria are equivalent to stability and costability.

At the point $[\lambda_1:\lambda_2:\mu_1:\mu_2]=[1:0:z_1:z_2]$, the displayed homogeneous maps reduce to $\alpha=a_z$ and $\beta=b_z^\dagger$. If the homogeneous maps have their monad ranks at every projective point, step 1.1 gives stability and step 1.2 gives costability.

Now suppose both moments vanish and the datum is regular. Step 1.1–1.2 give surjectivity of $b_z^\dagger$ and injectivity of $a_z$ for every finite $z$. Direct multiplication gives
$$b_z^\dagger a_z=\mu_{\mathbb C}=0,\qquad b_z^\dagger b_z-a_z^\dagger a_z=\mu_{\mathbb R}=0.$$
Hence $f_z=a_z^\dagger a_z=b_z^\dagger b_z$ is positive definite. On the real line over $z$, $\alpha=a_z\lambda_1+b_z\lambda_2$ and $\beta=b_z^\dagger\lambda_1-a_z^\dagger\lambda_2$; the cross Gram terms vanish by $b_z^\dagger a_z=0$, so $\alpha^\dagger\alpha=(|\lambda_1|^2+|\lambda_2|^2)f_z$ and $\beta\beta^\dagger=(|\lambda_1|^2+|\lambda_2|^2)f_z$. Therefore both maps have full rank whenever $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)\ne(0,0)$.

Every projective point with $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)\ne(0,0)$ lies on a unique real twistor line: after conjugating the second incidence equation, the system for $(z_1,\bar z_2)$ has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}\lambda_1&-\lambda_2\\\bar\lambda_2&\bar\lambda_1\end{pmatrix}$ and determinant $|\lambda_1|^2+|\lambda_2|^2>0$. On the line at infinity $(\lambda_1=\lambda_2=0)$ the maps are $\alpha=(-\mu_1,-\mu_2,0)^T$ and $\beta=(\mu_2,-\mu_1,0)$, which are injective and surjective respectively whenever $(\mu_1,\mu_2)\ne(0,0)$. Direct expansion gives
$$
\beta\alpha=\lambda_1^2\mu_{\mathbb C}+\lambda_1\lambda_2\mu_{\mathbb R}-\lambda_2^2\mu_{\mathbb C}^\dagger.
$$
Thus the maps have the required ranks everywhere and compose to zero, so they form a bundle monad.

If $k=0$, then $V=0$, every endomorphism and map to or from $V$ is the unique zero map, and the conditions of stability and costability both hold vacuously. The affine map $a_z:0\to W$ is injective and $b_z^\dagger:W\to0$ is surjective; the homogeneous source and target are zero, so their required ranks hold at every projective point. The moments vanish and the monad is $0\to W\otimes\mathcal O\to0$. This verifies the zero-dimensional boundary case without using an eigenvector argument on the zero space.

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $r\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, let
$X=\mathbb P^r(\mathbb C)=(\mathbb C^{r+1}\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb C^\times$
with its standard quotient complex-manifold structure, and let $E\to X$ be a
holomorphic vector bundle of finite rank.
Write $\mathcal O(E)$ for its sheaf of holomorphic sections, and let
$H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ denote the $q$th right-derived global-sections group of an
abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $X$. For
$0\le q\le r$, let $\mathcal A^{0,q}(E)$ be the sheaf of smooth sections of
$\Lambda^{0,q}T^*X\otimes_{\mathbb C}E$, where $\Lambda^{0,q}T^*X$ is the
$q$th exterior power of the antiholomorphic cotangent subbundle. In a
holomorphic local frame of $E$,
define $\bar\partial_E$ by applying the scalar $\bar\partial$ to each
coefficient form; holomorphic transition matrices make this definition
independent of frame, and $\bar\partial_E^2=0$. Set
$\mathcal A^{0,q}(E)=0$ for $q>r$ and define
$$H^q_{\bar\partial}(X,E):=\frac{\ker\bigl(\bar\partial_E:\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{0,q}(E))\to\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{0,q+1}(E))\bigr)}{\operatorname{im}\bigl(\bar\partial_E:\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{0,q-1}(E))\to\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{0,q}(E))\bigr)},$$
where $\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)$ denotes the group of sections of $\mathcal F$ over
$X$ and the denominator is zero for $q=0$. For every $q\ge0$, the canonical
comparison induced by the smooth Dolbeault resolution is an isomorphism
$$H^q(X,\mathcal O(E))\cong H^q_{\bar\partial}(X,E).$$
For the trivial line bundle $E=\mathcal O_X$ and $0\le r\le3$, this gives
$$H^0(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=\mathbb C,\qquad H^q(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=0\quad(q>0).$$
The scalar cohomology conclusion is obtained by the direct Laurent–Čech
calculation on the standard projective cover; no GAGA theorem, Kähler Hodge
theorem in dimensions above one, or arbitrary-coherent projective vanishing is
assumed.

let $i:H\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^r(\mathbb C)$ be inclusion. For every

$$0\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(m-1) \xrightarrow{\ \cdot Z_0\ }\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(m) \longrightarrow i_*\mathcal O_H(m)\longrightarrow0.$$
Here $i_*\mathcal O_H(m)$ assigns to an open set $U$ the holomorphic
sections of $\mathcal O_H(m)$ on $U\cap H$. Twisting the sequence with

$$0\to\mathcal F'\to\mathcal F\to\mathcal F''\to0$$
be a short exact sequence of abelian sheaves on a topological space $X$, and let
$H^q(X,-)$ be sheaf cohomology computed from the supplied functorial injective
resolution datum $I$ on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $m\ge1$. A **chart** on a topological space $X$ is a homeomorphism
$\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ from an open set $U\subseteq X$ onto an open subset of
$\mathbb C^m$ with its usual topology ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]);
two charts $\varphi,\psi$ are **holomorphically compatible** when the
transition maps $\psi\circ\varphi^{-1}$ and $\varphi\circ\psi^{-1}$ are
holomorphic on the open sets where they are defined
([[def-holomorphic-function-in-several-complex-variables]]). A **holomorphic
atlas** is a family of pairwise compatible charts whose domains cover $X$. A
**complex manifold of dimension $m$** is a nonempty Hausdorff
([[def-hausdorff-space]]) second-countable ([[def-second-countable-space]])
topological space carrying a holomorphic atlas; the same maximal-atlas argument
as for [[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]] applies verbatim with
$\mathbb C^m$ in place of $\mathbb C$: the union of a holomorphic atlas with all
charts compatible with it is again a holomorphic atlas, so one passes to the
unique maximal atlas and calls its members holomorphic charts. Each chart is a
homeomorphism onto an open subset of $\mathbb C^m\cong\mathbb R^{2m}$, so $X$ is
a topological manifold without boundary of real dimension $2m$
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]), and for connected $X$ the case
$m=1$ recovers Riemann surfaces ([[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]]).

A **holomorphic map** $f:X\to Y$ between complex manifolds is a continuous map
whose expression in every pair of holomorphic charts is holomorphic
([[def-holomorphic-map-and-complex-jacobian]]); equivalently, for every open
$V\subseteq Y$ and every holomorphic function $h$ on $V$, the function
$h\circ f$ is holomorphic on $f^{-1}(V)$. The forward implication is the
holomorphic chain rule; conversely apply this condition to the coordinate
functions of a chart on $Y$.

**Induced smooth structure and complex structure.** Holomorphic functions on
open subsets of $\mathbb C^m$ are smooth
([[cor-holomorphic-functions-in-several-variables-are-smooth]]), so every
holomorphic atlas is a smooth atlas ([[def-smooth-atlas]]) and $X$ is a smooth
manifold of real dimension $2m$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]) whose smooth charts
include the holomorphic ones. In holomorphic coordinates
$z_k=x_k+iy_k$ the **complex structure** is the endomorphism field $J$ of the
tangent bundle determined by $J\partial_{x_k}=\partial_{y_k}$ and
$J\partial_{y_k}=-\partial_{x_k}$; it satisfies $J^2=-\mathrm{id}$ and is
independent of the holomorphic chart, because a holomorphic transition map has
complex-linear differential ([[def-holomorphic-map-and-complex-jacobian]],
[[thm-chain-rule-for-holomorphic-maps-in-several-variables]]) and complex-linear
maps intertwine the two coordinate definitions of multiplication by $i$. A
**Hermitian metric** on $X$ is a Riemannian metric $g$
([[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]) satisfying
$g(Jv,Jw)=g(v,w)$ for all tangent vectors $v,w$; its Riemannian volume density
is written $\mu_g$ ([[def-riemannian-volume-density]]). The complex structure
makes each tangent space a complex vector space, so the tangent bundle is a
smooth complex vector bundle in the sense of
[[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]].

**Holomorphic vector bundles and Hermitian bundle metrics.** A **holomorphic
vector bundle of rank $r$** on $X$ is a smooth complex vector bundle
$\pi:E\to X$ of rank $r$
([[def-smooth-vector-bundle-rank-fibre-and-trivial-bundle]],
[[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]]) together with an open
cover $(V_\alpha)$ of $X$ and smooth local trivializations
$\theta_\alpha:E|_{V_\alpha}\to V_\alpha\times\mathbb C^r$ whose transition
matrices $g_{\alpha\beta}:V_\alpha\cap V_\beta\to\mathrm{GL}_r(\mathbb C)$,
defined by $\theta_\alpha\theta_\beta^{-1}(p,v)=(p,g_{\alpha\beta}(p)v)$, are
holomorphic. A **holomorphic frame** over an open set $V$ is a smooth
complex-linear trivialization whose transition matrices with the supplied
trivializations are holomorphic on every overlap. Changing holomorphic frame multiplies a local section by a
holomorphic matrix, hence a smooth local section is **holomorphic** exactly when
its representatives in holomorphic frames are holomorphic functions. A
**Hermitian metric** $h$ on $E$ is a smooth bundle metric
([[def-smooth-bundle-metric]]) whose fibre pairings are positive definite
Hermitian forms, linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the
second; the condition is frame-independent because the gauge freedom is
conjugation by a pointwise invertible matrix. Smooth sections are
$\Gamma(E)$ ([[def-smooth-section-local-section-and-support]]).

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let
$$
\mathcal O(-1)\otimes U\xrightarrow{\alpha}\mathcal O\otimes S\xrightarrow{\beta}\mathcal O(1)\otimes U'
$$
be a locally split linear monad on $\mathbb P^3(\mathbb C)$ with locally free middle cohomology $F$. Suppose a nondegenerate Hermitian form $H$ on $S$, linear in the first variable, satisfies $\beta(z)=\alpha(jz)^\dagger H$ for $j(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\mu_1,\mu_2)=(-\bar\lambda_2,\bar\lambda_1,-\bar\mu_2,\bar\mu_1)$. Assume $H^0(\mathbb P^3,\mathcal O)=\mathbb C$, $H^q(\mathbb P^3,\mathcal O(-1))=0$ for every $q\ge0$, and $H^0(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(-1))=0$. Define $L=\bigcap_i\ker\beta_i\subseteq S$ and $M=\sum_i\operatorname{im}\alpha_i\subseteq S$, where $\alpha(z)=\sum_i z_i\alpha_i$ and $\beta(z)=\sum_i z_i\beta_i$. If the induced Hermitian form on $H^0(F|_\ell)$ is positive definite for every $\sigma$-invariant real line $\ell$, with line form the constant value $x\mapsto b_x(s(x),t(\sigma x))$ from the preceding first-order real-structure definition, then $H^0(F)=L=M^{\perp_H}$, $H|_L$ is positive definite, and $S=L\oplus M$ is an $H$-orthogonal decomposition. The monad and its pairing split as the constant summand $L\otimes\mathcal O$ plus the reduced monad $U\otimes\mathcal O(-1)\to M\otimes\mathcal O\to U'\otimes\mathcal O(1)$; the reduced cohomology has no global sections and remains positive on every real line. The conclusion includes $U=0$, when $L=S$ and $M=0$.

Assume full AC. Then the analytic sheaf cohomology of $\mathcal O(-1)$ vanishes in every degree on $\mathbb P^r(\mathbb C)$ for $1\le r\le3$. The analytic cohomology of $\mathcal O(-2)$ vanishes in every degree on $\mathbb P^r(\mathbb C)$ for $r=2,3$. In particular, $H^0(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(-1))=0$ and $H^q(\mathbb P^3,\mathcal O(-2))=0$ for $q=0,1,2$. Let $m\ge1$. A **chart** on a topological space $X$ is a homeomorphism
$\varphi:U\to\varphi(U)$ from an open set $U\subseteq X$ onto an open subset of
$\mathbb C^m$ with its usual topology ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]);
two charts $\varphi,\psi$ are **holomorphically compatible** when the
transition maps $\psi\circ\varphi^{-1}$ and $\varphi\circ\psi^{-1}$ are
holomorphic on the open sets where they are defined
([[def-holomorphic-function-in-several-complex-variables]]). A **holomorphic
atlas** is a family of pairwise compatible charts whose domains cover $X$. A
**complex manifold of dimension $m$** is a nonempty Hausdorff
([[def-hausdorff-space]]) second-countable ([[def-second-countable-space]])
topological space carrying a holomorphic atlas; the same maximal-atlas argument
as for [[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]] applies verbatim with
$\mathbb C^m$ in place of $\mathbb C$: the union of a holomorphic atlas with all
charts compatible with it is again a holomorphic atlas, so one passes to the
unique maximal atlas and calls its members holomorphic charts. Each chart is a
homeomorphism onto an open subset of $\mathbb C^m\cong\mathbb R^{2m}$, so $X$ is
a topological manifold without boundary of real dimension $2m$
([[def-topological-manifold-without-boundary]]), and for connected $X$ the case
$m=1$ recovers Riemann surfaces ([[def-riemann-surface-and-holomorphic-atlas]]).

A **holomorphic map** $f:X\to Y$ between complex manifolds is a continuous map
whose expression in every pair of holomorphic charts is holomorphic
([[def-holomorphic-map-and-complex-jacobian]]); equivalently, for every open
$V\subseteq Y$ and every holomorphic function $h$ on $V$, the function
$h\circ f$ is holomorphic on $f^{-1}(V)$. The forward implication is the
holomorphic chain rule; conversely apply this condition to the coordinate
functions of a chart on $Y$.

**Induced smooth structure and complex structure.** Holomorphic functions on
open subsets of $\mathbb C^m$ are smooth
([[cor-holomorphic-functions-in-several-variables-are-smooth]]), so every
holomorphic atlas is a smooth atlas ([[def-smooth-atlas]]) and $X$ is a smooth
manifold of real dimension $2m$ ([[def-smooth-manifold]]) whose smooth charts
include the holomorphic ones. In holomorphic coordinates
$z_k=x_k+iy_k$ the **complex structure** is the endomorphism field $J$ of the
tangent bundle determined by $J\partial_{x_k}=\partial_{y_k}$ and
$J\partial_{y_k}=-\partial_{x_k}$; it satisfies $J^2=-\mathrm{id}$ and is
independent of the holomorphic chart, because a holomorphic transition map has
complex-linear differential ([[def-holomorphic-map-and-complex-jacobian]],
[[thm-chain-rule-for-holomorphic-maps-in-several-variables]]) and complex-linear
maps intertwine the two coordinate definitions of multiplication by $i$. A
**Hermitian metric** on $X$ is a Riemannian metric $g$
([[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]]) satisfying
$g(Jv,Jw)=g(v,w)$ for all tangent vectors $v,w$; its Riemannian volume density
is written $\mu_g$ ([[def-riemannian-volume-density]]). The complex structure
makes each tangent space a complex vector space, so the tangent bundle is a
smooth complex vector bundle in the sense of
[[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]].

**Holomorphic vector bundles and Hermitian bundle metrics.** A **holomorphic
vector bundle of rank $r$** on $X$ is a smooth complex vector bundle
$\pi:E\to X$ of rank $r$
([[def-smooth-vector-bundle-rank-fibre-and-trivial-bundle]],
[[def-complex-linear-and-compatible-bundle-connections]]) together with an open
cover $(V_\alpha)$ of $X$ and smooth local trivializations
$\theta_\alpha:E|_{V_\alpha}\to V_\alpha\times\mathbb C^r$ whose transition
matrices $g_{\alpha\beta}:V_\alpha\cap V_\beta\to\mathrm{GL}_r(\mathbb C)$,
defined by $\theta_\alpha\theta_\beta^{-1}(p,v)=(p,g_{\alpha\beta}(p)v)$, are
holomorphic. A **holomorphic frame** over an open set $V$ is a smooth
complex-linear trivialization whose transition matrices with the supplied
trivializations are holomorphic on every overlap. Changing holomorphic frame multiplies a local section by a
holomorphic matrix, hence a smooth local section is **holomorphic** exactly when
its representatives in holomorphic frames are holomorphic functions. A
**Hermitian metric** $h$ on $E$ is a smooth bundle metric
([[def-smooth-bundle-metric]]) whose fibre pairings are positive definite
Hermitian forms, linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the
second; the condition is frame-independent because the gauge freedom is
conjugation by a pointwise invertible matrix. Smooth sections are
$\Gamma(E)$ ([[def-smooth-section-local-section-and-support]]).

Assume the full Axiom of Choice. Let $r\in\{0,1,2,3\}$, let
$X=\mathbb P^r(\mathbb C)=(\mathbb C^{r+1}\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb C^\times$
with its standard quotient complex-manifold structure, and let $E\to X$ be a
holomorphic vector bundle of finite rank.
Write $\mathcal O(E)$ for its sheaf of holomorphic sections, and let
$H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ denote the $q$th right-derived global-sections group of an
abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $X$. For
$0\le q\le r$, let $\mathcal A^{0,q}(E)$ be the sheaf of smooth sections of
$\Lambda^{0,q}T^*X\otimes_{\mathbb C}E$, where $\Lambda^{0,q}T^*X$ is the
$q$th exterior power of the antiholomorphic cotangent subbundle. In a
holomorphic local frame of $E$,
define $\bar\partial_E$ by applying the scalar $\bar\partial$ to each
coefficient form; holomorphic transition matrices make this definition
independent of frame, and $\bar\partial_E^2=0$. Set
$\mathcal A^{0,q}(E)=0$ for $q>r$ and define
$$H^q_{\bar\partial}(X,E):=\frac{\ker\bigl(\bar\partial_E:\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{0,q}(E))\to\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{0,q+1}(E))\bigr)}{\operatorname{im}\bigl(\bar\partial_E:\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{0,q-1}(E))\to\Gamma(X,\mathcal A^{0,q}(E))\bigr)},$$
where $\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)$ denotes the group of sections of $\mathcal F$ over
$X$ and the denominator is zero for $q=0$. For every $q\ge0$, the canonical
comparison induced by the smooth Dolbeault resolution is an isomorphism
$$H^q(X,\mathcal O(E))\cong H^q_{\bar\partial}(X,E).$$
For the trivial line bundle $E=\mathcal O_X$ and $0\le r\le3$, this gives
$$H^0(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=\mathbb C,\qquad H^q(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=0\quad(q>0).$$
The scalar cohomology conclusion is obtained by the direct Laurent–Čech
calculation on the standard projective cover; no GAGA theorem, Kähler Hodge
theorem in dimensions above one, or arbitrary-coherent projective vanishing is
assumed.

e0$, while $ eta(a,b)A_zv=0$ for every $(a,b)$. Its class is a global section of the holomorphically trivial bundle $F_M|_\ell$ vanishing at $(1,0)$. Use the constant Hermitian matrix $H$ on $S=M$ for the following positivity calculation. Put $z_1=x_1+ix_2$, $z_2=x_3+ix_4$ and $$a(x)=\alpha(1,0,z_1,z_2)=a_0+z_1M_1+z_2M_2,\qquad b(x)=\alpha(0,1,-\bar z_2,\bar z_1)=b_0-\bar z_2M_1+\bar z_1M_2.$$ The two arguments are $z,jz$ in the stated coordinate convention. Step 1.1 gives $$a^\dagger Ha=b^\dagger Hb=A(x),\qquad a^\dagger Hb=0,$$ with $A(x)$ invertible for every $x$. Apply the same identities on the infinity line with $z=(0,0,1,0)$ and $jz=(0,0,0,1)$ to obtain $$M_1^\dagger HM_1=M_2^\dagger HM_2=C,\qquad M_1^\dagger HM_2=0,$$ where $C$ is invertible. Thus $y^\dagger HQy=(Qy)^\dagger H(Qy)\ge0$ for every $y$, by the actual induced section pairing there. This identification uses the lifted identity $\beta=\alpha(jz)^\dagger H$ and the Euler-complex decomposition of step 2.1; it is not an extra assumption of positivity of $H$ on the coefficient images.

Put $P=a^\dagger HM_1$ and $R=a^\dagger HM_2$. Since $a_\mu=(M_1,iM_1,M_2,iM_2)$, the derivatives of $A$ are $$A_1=P+P^\dagger,\quad A_2=iP-iP^\dagger,\quad A_3=R+R^\dagger,\quad A_4=iR-iR^\dagger.$$ Pairing the real and imaginary derivatives, with the matrix order retained, gives $$\sum_\mu A_\mu K A_\mu =2(PKP^\dagger+P^\dagger KP+RKR^\dagger+R^\dagger KR) =\sum_\mu a_\mu^\dagger H(1-Q)a_\mu.$$ The second equality follows by substituting $1-Q=aKa^\dagger H+bKb^\dagger H$ and the displayed formulas for $b^\dagger HM_i$. Expanding the Gram gives $A(x)=|x|^2C+O(|x|)$ uniformly in direction. Suppose a nondegenerate Hermitian form $H$ on $S$, linear in the first variable, satisfies $\beta(z)=\alpha(jz)^\dagger H$ for $j(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\mu_1,\mu_2)=(-\bar\lambda_2,\bar\lambda_1,-\bar\mu_2,\bar\mu_1)$. Assume $H^0(\mathbb P^3,\mathcal O)=\mathbb C$, $H^q(\mathbb P^3,\mathcal O(-1))=0$ for every $q\ge0$, and $H^0(\mathbb P^1,\mathcal O(-1))=0$. Define $L=\bigcap_i\ker\beta_i\subseteq S$ and $M=\sum_i\operatorname{im}\alpha_i\subseteq S$, where $\alpha(z)=\sum_i z_i\alpha_i$ and $\beta(z)=\sum_i z_i\beta_i$. If the induced Hermitian form on $H^0(F|_\ell)$ is positive definite for every $\sigma$-invariant real line $\ell$, with line form the constant value $x\mapsto b_x(s(x),t(\sigma x))$ from the preceding first-order real-structure definition, then $H^0(F)=L=M^{\perp_H}$, $H|_L$ is positive definite, and $S=L\oplus M$ is an $H$-orthogonal decomposition. The monad and its pairing split as the constant summand $L\otimes\mathcal O$ plus the reduced monad $U\otimes\mathcal O(-1)\to M\otimes\mathcal O\to U'\otimes\mathcal O(1)$; the reduced cohomology has no global sections and remains positive on every real line. The conclusion includes $U=0$, when $L=S$ and $M=0$.

Let $M$ be the coefficient-image subspace of a linear monad on $\mathbb P^3(\mathbb C)$ after removing its constant orthogonal summand as in the preceding splitting lemma. Thus its reduced middle cohomology has no global sections, is trivial on every $\sigma$-invariant real line, and has a positive section pairing on each such line. Let $H$ be the induced nondegenerate Hermitian form on $M$, linear in the first variable, and suppose $\beta(z)=\alpha(jz)^\dagger H$ and $\beta(z)\alpha(z)=0$ for every $z\in\mathbb C^4$, with $j^2=-1$. Then $H$ is positive definite on all of $M$.

Fix integers $N\ge1$ and $k\ge0$ and equip $V=\mathbb C^k$ and $W=\mathbb C^N$ with the standard Hermitian inner products $\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_j\overline{u_j}v_j$, which are conjugate-linear in the first variable. For a linear map $T:E\to F$ between these spaces, its Hermitian adjoint $T^\dagger:F\to E$ is characterized by $\langle Tu,v\rangle_F=\langle u,T^\dagger v\rangle_E$; in the standard bases its matrix is the conjugate transpose. For $A,B\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$, define their commutator by $[A,B]:=AB-BA$. Let

$$\mathscr D_{k,N}=\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)^2\times\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(W,V)\times\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(V,W),\qquad \operatorname{Herm}(V)=\{H\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V):H^\dagger=H\}.$$

Here $\operatorname{Herm}(V)$ is regarded as a real vector space. A framed ADHM linear datum is $x=(B_1,B_2,I,J)\in\mathscr D_{k,N}$. The complex and real moment maps are the maps $\mu_{\mathbb C}:\mathscr D_{k,N}\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)$ and $\mu_{\mathbb R}:\mathscr D_{k,N}\to\operatorname{Herm}(V)$ defined by

$$\mu_{\mathbb C}(x)=[B_1,B_2]+IJ,\qquad \mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J.$$

The datum is stable if the vectors $B_{i_1}\cdots B_{i_m}I(w)$, with $m\ge0$, $i_j\in\{1,2\}$ and $w\in W$, span $V$. It is costable if there is no nonzero subspace of $V$ invariant under both $B_i$ and contained in $\ker J$. It is regular if it is stable and costable. The group $GL(V)$ acts by $g\cdot x=(gB_1g^{-1},gB_2g^{-1},gI,Jg^{-1})$. Its unitary subgroup is $U(V)$.

Write $X^s=\{x:\mu_{\mathbb C}(x)=0,\ x\text{ stable}\}$, $X^{\mathrm{reg}}=\{x\in X^s:x\text{ costable}\}$ and, for real $\zeta\ge0$, $X_\zeta^U=\{x\in X^s:\mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=\zeta I_V\}$. Denote the corresponding orbit sets by $X^s/GL(V)$, $X^{\mathrm{reg}}/GL(V)$ and $X_\zeta^U/U(V)$, with quotient topologies when discussing their analytic spaces. A word frame consists of $k$ columns obtained by fixed words in $B_1,B_2$ applied to fixed standard basis vectors of $W$.

For $T_{\mathbb C}=(\mathbb C^*)^2\times(\mathbb C^*)^N$, write $t_1,t_2,e_1,\ldots,e_N$ for the coordinate characters and put $h=\operatorname{diag}(e_1^{-1},\ldots,e_N^{-1})$. Its action is $(t_1,t_2,h)\cdot x=(t_1B_1,t_2B_2,Ih^{-1},t_1t_2hJ)$. The compact torus is its subgroup on which all characters have modulus one. The framing representation thus has character $\sum_\alpha e_\alpha^{-1}$ and its dual has character $\sum_\alpha e_\alpha$.

These are finite-dimensional matrix definitions. They do not assert a real/complex quotient correspondence, a sheaf or ASD identification, or a noncompact pushforward. In particular, positive-FI stability and zero-FI regularity are distinct conditions; neither an endpoint identification nor an ordinary ASD interpretation follows from this definition.

Fix integers $N\ge1$ and $k\ge0$. Let $V=\mathbb C^k$, $W=\mathbb C^N$, and let $B_1,B_2\in\operatorname{End}(V)$, $I:W\to V$, $J:V\to W$ satisfy $[B_1,B_2]+IJ=0$. Define for $z=(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^2$
$$a_z=(B_1-z_1,\ B_2-z_2,\ J)^T:V\to V\oplus V\oplus W,\qquad b_z^\dagger=(-B_2+z_2,\ B_1-z_1,\ I):V\oplus V\oplus W\to V.$$
Then $a_z$ is injective for every $z$ if and only if the datum is costable, and $b_z^\dagger$ is surjective for every $z$ if and only if the datum is stable, where stability and costability have their word-span and invariant-subspace meanings. For the homogeneous linear maps
$$
\alpha=(B_1\lambda_1-B_2^\dagger\lambda_2-\mu_1,\ B_2\lambda_1+B_1^\dagger\lambda_2-\mu_2,\ J\lambda_1+I^\dagger\lambda_2)^T,
$$
$$\beta=(-C,\ A,\ I\lambda_1-J^\dagger\lambda_2),\quad A=B_1\lambda_1-B_2^\dagger\lambda_2-\mu_1,\quad C=B_2\lambda_1+B_1^\dagger\lambda_2-\mu_2,$$
fiberwise injectivity of $\alpha$ and surjectivity of $\beta$ on $\mathbb P^3$ imply regularity. Conversely, if the datum is regular and both raw moment maps vanish, then these homogeneous maps are fiberwise injective and surjective and form a linear bundle monad.

Use the dual-number scheme, relative projective-space charts, finite locally free sheaves and twisting sheaves as defined, respectively, in the four suppliers listed under Definition references, with the inherited AC convention for the twisting-sheaf construction. Let $A=\mathbb C[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$ and equip it with the conjugate-linear involution $\overline{a+b\epsilon}=\bar a+\bar b\epsilon$. Its reduction is the quotient map $A\to\mathbb C$ sending $\epsilon$ to zero. For every $r\in\mathbb R$, the map $\rho_r:A\to A$ fixing $\mathbb C$ and sending $\epsilon$ to $r\epsilon$ preserves this involution.

A **first-order family of positive real linear monads of dimensions $(k,2k+N,k)$** is a three-term complex of locally free sheaves on $\mathbb P^3_A=\operatorname{Proj}A[\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\mu_1,\mu_2]$,
$$\mathcal O(-1)\otimes_A U_A\xrightarrow{\alpha_A}\mathcal O\otimes_A S_A\xrightarrow{\beta_A}\mathcal O(1)\otimes_A U'_A,$$
where $U_A,S_A,U'_A$ are free $A$-modules of ranks $k,2k+N,k$, each map is homogeneous linear in $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\mu_1,\mu_2)$, $\beta_A\alpha_A=0$, $\alpha_A$ is a locally split injection, $\beta_A$ is a locally split surjection, and $F_A=\ker\beta_A/\operatorname{im}\alpha_A$ is locally free of rank $N$. The two short exact sequences defined by the kernel and image split locally; hence their formation and the middle cohomology commute with reduction $A\to\mathbb C$. The reduced complex is therefore an ordinary linear monad on $\mathbb P^3_\mathbb C$.

The **first-order locally-free/base-change range** used here further requires that $H^0(\mathbb P^3_A,F_A)$ is a free $A$-module and reduction identifies it with $H^0(\mathbb P^3_\mathbb C,F_0)$, where $F_0=F_A\otimes_A\mathbb C$. The image in $S_A$ of the map from the four coefficient copies of $U_A$ under $\alpha_A$ is a direct summand and reduces to the corresponding coefficient-image subspace of $S_0$. For each real twistor line $\ell$ in the reduced projective space, the restriction of $F_A$ to $\ell_A=\ell\times_{\mathbb C}\operatorname{Spec}A$ is trivial of rank $N$, and reduction identifies its global sections with $H^0(\ell,F_0|_\ell)$. These conditions state the precise global, coefficient-image, and line-section base-change range; no arbitrary analytic family or algebraization assertion is included.

Extend the coordinate map $j(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\mu_1,\mu_2)=(-\bar\lambda_2,\bar\lambda_1,-\bar\mu_2,\bar\mu_1)$ semilinearly using the involution of $A$; write $\widetilde\sigma$ for its projective action over $A$ and $\sigma$ for its reduction. Since $j^2=-1$, both projective actions square to the identity and preserve each real twistor line. A **real twistor line** means the projectivization of a $j$-invariant complex two-plane in $\mathbb C^4$. Equivalently these are the finite lines
$$\mu_1=z_1\lambda_1-\bar z_2\lambda_2,\qquad \mu_2=z_2\lambda_1+\bar z_1\lambda_2,\qquad (z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^2,$$
together with $\ell_\infty=\{\lambda_1=\lambda_2=0\}$. Indeed a nonzero vector $v$ and $jv$ are complex-linearly independent because $j^2=-1$; they span the invariant plane. If its $\lambda$ projection is nonzero, that projection and its quaternionic conjugate give an invertible two-by-two matrix with determinant $|\lambda_1|^2+|\lambda_2|^2$, so it has exactly the displayed graph form; if the projection is zero the plane is the $\mu$ plane. Each fixed-line restriction above means the corresponding constant thickening $\ell_A$.

For an $A$-locally free sheaf $G$, write $D_A(G):=(\widetilde\sigma^*\overline G)^\vee$, where $\overline G$ has its scalar action conjugated by $a\mapsto\bar a$ and $(-)^\vee=\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal O}(-,\mathcal O)$. On the reduction, write $D(F_0):=(\sigma^*\overline{F_0})^\vee$. A first-order real structure is an $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^3_A}$-linear isomorphism $h_A:F_A\to D_A(F_A)$ fixed by the canonical double-dual identification $D_A^2(F_A)\cong F_A$. Its reduction $h_0:F_0\to D(F_0)$ gives fiber pairings
$$b_x(v,w):=h_{0,x}(v)(\overline w),\qquad v\in(F_0)_x,\quad w\in(F_0)_{\sigma x},$$
which are linear in $v$, conjugate-linear in $w$, and satisfy $b_{\sigma x}(w,v)=\overline{b_x(v,w)}$. For a $\sigma$-invariant real line $\ell$ and $s,t\in H^0(\ell,F_0|_\ell)$, the induced line form is the constant value of the function $x\mapsto b_x(s(x),t(\sigma x))$; constancy is part of the stated real-structure condition. It is first-slot-linear and Hermitian by the displayed symmetry. Positivity means $b_\ell(s,s)>0$ for every nonzero $s$. A unitary framing at infinity is an isometric isomorphism $F_A|_{\ell_\infty}\cong (A\otimes_\mathbb C W)\otimes_A\mathcal O_{\ell_\infty}$, where $\ell_\infty=\{\lambda_1=\lambda_2=0\}$ and $W=\mathbb C^N$ has its standard first-slot-linear Hermitian form.

An isomorphism of such families is an $A$-linear chain isomorphism that intertwines the $\sigma$-Hermitian pairings and the framing. No order or positivity is assigned to elements of $A$ with nonzero nilpotent part: positivity is required only after reduction. The base-change scope in this definition consists exactly of reduction $\epsilon\mapsto0$ and the involution-preserving maps $\rho_r$ for real $r$.

Let $k,N\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}$, and let $\mathcal F$ be the locally free algebraic middle cohomology of a linear monad
$$
\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^3}(-1)^{\oplus k}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^3}^{\oplus(2k+N)}\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^3}(1)^{\oplus k}
$$
on $\mathbb P^3_\mathbb C$, with exactness at both ends.

For algebraic sheaf cohomology, write $H^q(\mathbb P^3,\mathcal G)$ for the right-derived global-sections group. If these groups are finite-dimensional and vanish for all sufficiently large $q$, define the algebraic Euler characteristic by $\chi(\mathcal G)=\sum_{q\ge0}(-1)^q\dim_{\mathbb C}H^q(\mathbb P^3,\mathcal G)$. Let $H_{\rm alg}=c_1^{\rm alg}(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^3}(1))$ in the Chow ring and let $H_{\rm top}=c_1^{\rm top}(\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^3}(1))$ in singular cohomology. The hyperplane cycle map $\operatorname{cl}:A^1(\mathbb P^3)\to H^2(\mathbb P^3;\mathbb Z)$ identifies $H_{\rm alg}$ with $H_{\rm top}$; write $H$ for either class in the corresponding formula. The algebraic Chern character is $N-kH_{\rm alg}^2$, the algebraic first Chern class is zero, the algebraic second Chern class is $kH_{\rm alg}^2$, and the algebraic Euler characteristic is $N-2k$. The analytification of $\mathcal F$ has total topological Chern class $1+kH_{\rm top}^2$ through degree six and topological Chern character $N-kH_{\rm top}^2$.

Let $\jmath:\mathbb C^4\to\mathbb C^4$ be the conjugate-linear map
$$\jmath(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\mu_1,\mu_2)=(-\bar\lambda_2,\bar\lambda_1,-\bar\mu_2,\bar\mu_1),\qquad \jmath^2=-1.$$
Use $\mathbb H=\mathbb C\oplus\mathbb C\mathbf j$, where $\mathbf j^2=-1$ and $\mathbf j a=\bar a\mathbf j$ for $a\in\mathbb C$, and identify $\mathbb C^4$ with the right quaternionic vector space $\mathbb H^2$ by
$$ (\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\mu_1,\mu_2)\longmapsto(\lambda_1+\bar\lambda_2\mathbf j,\ \mu_1+\bar\mu_2\mathbf j).$$
Under this identification, right multiplication by $\mathbf j$ is $\jmath$. Give $\mathbb H\mathbb P^1=(\mathbb H^2\setminus\{0\})/\mathbb H^\times$ its standard smooth quotient structure; it is the 4-sphere and its points are the one-dimensional right-$\mathbb H$ subspaces of $\mathbb H^2$. The **quaternionic quotient map** is the smooth map
$$\pi:\mathbb P(\mathbb C^4)\longrightarrow\mathbb H\mathbb P^1,\qquad [\lambda_1:\lambda_2:\mu_1:\mu_2]\longmapsto[(\lambda_1+\bar\lambda_2\mathbf j,\ \mu_1+\bar\mu_2\mathbf j)]_{\mathbb H}.$$
Equivalently, $\pi([v])=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}(v,\jmath v)$, a $\jmath$-invariant complex two-plane. This is well-defined because $\jmath(cv)=\bar c\,\jmath v$ for $c\in\mathbb C$ and $v,\jmath v$ are complex-linearly independent when $v\ne0$ and $\jmath^2=-1$. Its fiber over a quaternionic line $L$ is $\mathbb P_{\mathbb C}(L)\cong\mathbb P^1(\mathbb C)$. In the finite chart with $\lambda=\lambda_1+\bar\lambda_2\mathbf j\ne0$ and $z=\mu\lambda^{-1}=z_1+\bar z_2\mathbf j$, the fiber equations are
$$\mu_1=z_1\lambda_1-\bar z_2\lambda_2,\qquad \mu_2=z_2\lambda_1+\bar z_1\lambda_2,$$
and the fiber over the remaining point is $\ell_\infty=\{\lambda_1=\lambda_2=0\}$. Orient each fiber by its complex orientation. Write $z_1=x^0+ix^1$ and $z_2=x^2+ix^3$, so the chart orientation is $dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$; orient $S^4$ so this positive stereographic chart followed by the fiber orientation induces the complex orientation of $\mathbb P^3$. Since the base and fiber dimensions are $4$ and $2$, respectively, reversing these orientation factors has sign $(-1)^{4\cdot2}=+1$, so this also agrees with the fiber-first convention. Let $u\in H^4(S^4;\mathbb Z)$ be the positive point class for this orientation. Then $\pi^*u=H_{\rm top}^2$. Consequently, if the underlying topological bundle of $\mathcal F$ is $\pi^*E$ for a rank-$N$ complex bundle $E\to S^4$ with $c_1(E)=0$, then $c_2(E)=ku$ and $\langle c_2(E),[S^4]\rangle=k$.

Assume AC. Fix $N\ge1$, $k\ge0$, standard Hermitian $V=\mathbb C^k$, $W=\mathbb C^N$ and ADHM data $x=(B_1,B_2,I,J)$ with the complex equation $[B_1,B_2]+IJ=0$. Stability means that the $B_1,B_2$ words applied to $I(W)$ span $V$; costability means no nonzero common invariant subspace of $V$ lies in $\ker J$; regular means both. Set

$$\mu_{\mathbb R}(x)=[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J.$$

For every $\zeta>0$, each stable $GL(V)$ orbit meets $\mu_{\mathbb R}=\zeta I_V$ in exactly one $U(V)$ orbit, and the inclusion induces a diffeomorphism of smooth real manifolds

$$\{\mu_{\mathbb C}=0,\ \mu_{\mathbb R}=\zeta I_V,\ \mathrm{stable}\}/U(V)\ \cong\ X^s/GL(V).$$

At $\zeta=0$, every stable datum satisfying the real equation is automatically costable. Each regular complex orbit meets the zero real level in exactly one unitary orbit, giving instead

$$\{\mu_{\mathbb C}=0,\ \mu_{\mathbb R}=0,\ \mathrm{stable}\}/U(V)\ \cong\ X^{\mathrm{reg}}/GL(V).$$

Both identifications are equivariant for the compact rotation/framing torus in the raw-data convention. For $k=0$ all spaces are points. This theorem identifies the stated finite-dimensional quotients; it asserts no correspondence with sheaves or ASD connections, and no identification of the entire positive-FI quotient with the zero-FI regular locus.

For $r\ge1$, let $H=\{[Z_0:\cdots:Z_r]\in\mathbb P^r(\mathbb C):Z_0=0\}$ and
let $i:H\hookrightarrow\mathbb P^r(\mathbb C)$ be inclusion. For every
integer $m$, the homogeneous coordinate $Z_0$ defines an exact sequence of
holomorphic sheaves
$$0\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(m-1) \xrightarrow{\ \cdot Z_0\ }\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(m) \longrightarrow i_*\mathcal O_H(m)\longrightarrow0.$$
Here $i_*\mathcal O_H(m)$ assigns to an open set $U$ the holomorphic
sections of $\mathcal O_H(m)$ on $U\cap H$. Twisting the sequence with
$m=0$ by $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(-1)$ gives, in particular,
$$0\longrightarrow\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(-2) \longrightarrow\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^r}(-1) \longrightarrow i_*\mathcal O_H(-1)\longrightarrow0.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $A$ be a commutative
ring with $1$ ([[def-commutative-ring]]), let $n\ge0$, let $d\in\mathbb Z$ and
let $X=\mathbb P^n_A\cong\operatorname{Proj}A[x_0,\dots,x_n]$ be relative
projective space ([[def-relative-projective-space-standard-charts]],
[[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]]), with twisting sheaf
$\mathcal O_X(d)$ ([[def-twisting-sheaf-proj]]) and cohomology
$H^q(X,\mathcal O_X(d))$. Then
$$H^q(X,\mathcal O_X(d))=0\qquad\text{unless }q=0\text{ or }q=n.$$
If $n>0$, then $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(d))\cong A[x_0,\dots,x_n]_d$ when $d\ge0$
and $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(d))=0$ when $d<0$, where
$A[x_0,\dots,x_n]_d$ is the degree-$d$ graded piece
([[def-graded-ring-and-graded-module]]); and $H^n(X,\mathcal O_X(d))$ is the
free $A$-module on the Laurent monomials $x_0^{e_0}\cdots x_n^{e_n}$ with
$e_i<0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_ie_i=d$, so that it is nonzero precisely when
$d\le-n-1$ and $A\ne0$. For $n=0$ one has $\mathbb P^0_A=\operatorname{Spec}A$
and $H^0(X,\mathcal O_X(d))\cong A$ for every $d\in\mathbb Z$, with all higher
groups zero. The zero ring $A=0$ is allowed: then $X=\varnothing$ and all
groups are zero, in agreement with both displayed descriptions.

derivations.claim: First the holomorphic monad maps have homogeneous linear entries. Indeed, in the $m=1$ sequence of [F10], $H^1(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O)=0$ by [A1], so restriction $H^0(\mathbb P^r,\mathcal O(1))\to H^0(\mathbb P^{r-1},\mathcal O(1))$ is surjective and its kernel is the defining hyperplane coordinate times $H^0(\mathcal O)=\mathbb C$. Starting with $r=0$, where $\mathcal O(1)$ on a point has one-dimensional section space, induction shows that every section is a linear combination of the homogeneous coordinates: subtract the global coordinate lifts of its restriction, then the remaining section is a constant multiple of the defining coordinate. This applies to entries of both $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal O(-1),\mathcal O)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal O,\mathcal O(1))$. Thus no algebraic/analytic comparison is needed to introduce their four coefficient maps. By [A1] and [F9], the hyperplane sequences and analytic scalar theorem give exactly the negative-twist vanishings required by [F1]. Apply [F1] to the pairing isomorphism; it gives the unique constant Hermitian lift $H$ with the signed identities there. Thus no algebraic cohomology group is being substituted for the analytic lifting groups.

The first-order families here are the algebraic locally free sheaves on $\mathbb P^3_A$ specified in [F6]. The algebraic cohomology calculation [F11] gives $H^0(\mathbb P^3_A,\mathcal O)=A$ and the required vanishing of $\mathcal O(-1)$ and $\mathcal O(-2)$ over $A$, with the monomial modules and maps commuting with coefficient homomorphisms. The lifting calculation in [F1] uses only locally split kernel/image sequences, the long exact sequence, these cohomology groups, and the fact that global maps between equal twists are their constant coefficient matrices. The same calculation over $A$ therefore lifts the family pairing uniquely to an $A$-linear constant chain isomorphism with Hermitian middle matrix $H_A$; its inverse exists because its reduction is invertible. In both kernel/image sequences the vanishings identify $H^0(F_A)$ with the constant coefficient kernel $L_A$ of $\beta_A$. The specified global-section base-change condition makes the reduction of $L_A\hookrightarrow S_A$ injective; a full-rank minor is then a unit, so $L_A$ is a direct summand.

By [F2], the global constant subspace $L$ is positive and $S=L\oplus M$ orthogonally, and the reduced monad on $M$ preserves the full framing. Apply [F3] to that reduced monad; it proves $H|_M$ positive. Since $H|_L$ is positive and the sum is orthogonal, $H$ is positive definite on all of $S$. In particular the argument also covers $k=0$, where $M=0$.

By hypothesis the coefficient-image module $M_A$ is a direct summand. The coefficient identities give $M_A^\perp=L_A$; for a direct summand in a finite free module with a perfect pairing, the restriction map to its dual is split-surjective, so taking orthogonal complements twice returns that summand. Hence $M_A=L_A^\perp$ and $S_A=L_A\oplus M_A$. For each reduced real line $\ell$, its $\jmath$-invariant two-plane gives $\ell\cong\mathbb P^1_{\mathbb C}$ and $\ell_A\cong\mathbb P^1_A$. The restricted kernel/image sequence has kernel term $U_A\otimes_A\mathcal O_{\ell_A}(-1)$; by [F11], $H^0(\ell_A,\mathcal O_{\ell_A}(-1))=0$. Thus global sections of $K_A|_{\ell_A}$ inject into those of $F_A|_{\ell_A}$. A constant vector $l\in L_A\subseteq S_A$ gives a section of $K_A|_{\ell_A}$, and if its image in $H^0(\ell_A,F_A|_{\ell_A})$ vanishes then that section, and hence $l$, vanishes. The line-section base-change hypothesis identifies the reduced section space, so the reduced line positivity gives positivity on $L_0$. The internal-positivity proof applies to the reduction on $M_0$, so its reduced form is positive too. On infinity the family framing identifies the remaining orthogonal complement isometrically with $W_A$.

Write the four coefficient maps of $\alpha$ as $P=\alpha_{\lambda_1}$, $Q=\alpha_{\lambda_2}$, $R=\alpha_{\mu_1}$, and $T=\alpha_{\mu_2}$. From the first-slot convention and $j^2=-1$, the corresponding coefficients of $\beta$ are $Q^\dagger H,-P^\dagger H,T^\dagger H,-R^\dagger H$ in that order. The $\mu_1^2,\mu_2^2,\mu_1\mu_2$ coefficients of $\beta\alpha=0$ give $T^\dagger HR=R^\dagger HT=0$ and $R^\dagger HR=T^\dagger HT$. The maps $R,T$ are injective by exactness at the two coordinate points of $\ell_\infty$. Positivity of $H$ therefore makes their common Gram matrix $G$ positive definite. Replacing the paired end bases by $G^{-1/2}$ normalizes both maps to isometries with orthogonal images. Choosing an orthonormal basis of $S$ then identifies $R=-\iota_1$, $T=-\iota_2$ and $S=(V\oplus V)\oplus W_0$, with $W_0$ their orthogonal complement.

At infinity the maps are $\alpha_\infty=-\mu_1\iota_1-\mu_2\iota_2$ and $\beta_\infty=\mu_2\iota_1^\dagger-\mu_1\iota_2^\dagger$. For every $[\mu_1:\mu_2]\in\mathbb P^1$, the kernel of $\beta_\infty$ in $V\oplus V$ is the line-valued copy $\{(\mu_1v,\mu_2v):v\in V\}$, which is exactly the image of $\alpha_\infty$; $W_0$ is killed by $\beta_\infty$ and meets that image trivially. Therefore the restricted cohomology and its section pairing are canonically $W_0\otimes\mathcal O_{\ell_\infty}$ and its standard positive form. The specified unitary framing identifies $W_0$ with $W$ without discarding any flat summand.

Relative to $S=V\oplus V\oplus W$, write $P=(B_1,B_2,J)^T$ and $Q=(Q_1,Q_2,Q_W)^T$. The coefficient of $\lambda_1\mu_1$ in $\beta\alpha=0$ is $Q^\dagger HR+T^\dagger HP=0$, so $Q_1=-B_2^\dagger$; the coefficient of $\lambda_1\mu_2$ is $Q^\dagger HT-R^\dagger HP=0$, so $Q_2=B_1^\dagger$. Define $I^\dagger=Q_W$. These definitions give exactly the displayed $\alpha$ and, by the lifted reality identity, the displayed $\beta$.

The $\lambda_1^2$ coefficient of $\beta\alpha=0$ is $Q^\dagger HP=0$. Substitution of the blocks gives $-[B_2,B_1]+IJ=[B_1,B_2]+IJ=0$. The $\lambda_1\lambda_2$ coefficient is $Q^\dagger HQ-P^\dagger HP=0$. Expanding it gives $[B_1,B_1^\dagger]+[B_2,B_2^\dagger]+II^\dagger-J^\dagger J=0$, which is $\mu_{\mathbb R}=0$. Conversely, these two moment equations make all coefficients of $\beta\alpha$ vanish, and direct substitution yields $$\beta\alpha=\lambda_1^2\mu_{\mathbb C} +\lambda_1\lambda_2\mu_{\mathbb R} -\lambda_2^2\mu_{\mathbb C}^\dagger=0.$$

$$\mathscr D_{k,N}=\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V)^2\times\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(W,V)\times\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(V,W),\qquad \operatorname{Herm}(V)=\{H\in\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(V):H^\dagger=H\}.$$

Let $u\in H^4(S^4;\mathbb Z)$ be the positive point class for this orientation. Then $\pi^*u=H_{\rm top}^2$. Consequently, if the underlying topological bundle of $\mathcal F$ is $\pi^*E$ for a rank-$N$ complex bundle $E\to S^4$ with $c_1(E)=0$, then $c_2(E)=ku$ and $\langle c_2(E),[S^4]\rangle=k$.

Let $E\to M$ be a smooth vector bundle with connection $\nabla$. For smooth
vector fields $X,Y$ and a smooth section $s$ of $E$, the **curvature of
$\nabla$** is

$$R^\nabla(X,Y)s:=\nabla_X\nabla_Ys-\nabla_Y\nabla_Xs-\nabla_{[X,Y]}s.$$

This uses the same sign convention as the curvature of an affine connection.
The next proposition proves that this operator is tensorial and hence is an
$\operatorname{End}(E)$-valued two-form. At this definition stage no metric,
torsion, or bundle trivialization is assumed.

If $M$ is empty, $E$ has rank zero, or $M$ has dimension zero, the displayed
operator is the unique zero curvature operator. For a rank-one bundle and for
a manifold with boundary the same local formula applies without modification.

derivations.claim:
Since $B_1=B_2=0$, one has
$\mu_{\mathbb C}=IJ=(\rho,0)(0,\rho)^T=0$ and
$\mu_{\mathbb R}=II^\dagger-J^\dagger J=\rho^2-\rho^2=0$.
The nonzero map $I$ has image $V$, so its word span is $V$ and the datum is
stable. The nonzero map $J:V\to W$ is injective, so $\ker J=0$ and the datum
is costable. Thus it is regular.

Substitution in the raw homogeneous formulas gives the displayed
$\alpha$ and $\beta$. Direct multiplication gives
$\beta\alpha=-\mu_1\mu_2+\mu_1\mu_2+\rho^2\lambda_1\lambda_2
-\rho^2\lambda_1\lambda_2=0$, equivalently the zero-moment polynomial in
[F2]. At infinity these maps restrict to
$\alpha=(-\mu_1,-\mu_2,0,0)^T$ and
$\beta=(\mu_2,-\mu_1,0,0)$, whose middle cohomology is the last two
coordinates $W$ with its identity framing. The middle standard Hermitian
form is positive.

On the real line over $z$, the incidence equations give
$\alpha=a_z\lambda_1+b_z\lambda_2$ and
$\beta=b_z^\dagger\lambda_1-a_z^\dagger\lambda_2$, where
$$a_z=(-z_1,-z_2,0,\rho)^T,\qquad b_z=(\bar z_2,-\bar z_1,\rho,0)^T.$$
Multiplication gives $a_z^\dagger a_z=b_z^\dagger b_z=f_z$ and
$b_z^\dagger a_z=0$. Thus $a_z,b_z$ are orthogonal isometric copies after
rescaling by $f_z^{-1/2}$. Their common orthogonal complement
$E_z=(\operatorname{im}a_z\oplus\operatorname{im}b_z)^\perp$ has dimension
two. The line complex on the first two copies is the Euler complex
$V\mathcal O(-1)\to(V\oplus V)\mathcal O\to V\mathcal O(1)$ and is exact at
its ends with zero middle cohomology; the complementary term is
$E_z\mathcal O$. Hence the line bundle is trivial and its section pairing
is the standard positive form on $E_z$. Since $D_z$ has rows
$b_z^\dagger,a_z^\dagger$, $E_z=\ker D_z$. Finally direct multiplication
gives $D_zD_z^\dagger=f_z I_2$; because $\rho>0$, $f_z>0$ at every $z$.

The matrix $P_z=I_4-D_z^\dagger f_z^{-1}D_z$ is Hermitian and
$P_z^2=P_z$, since $D_zD_z^\dagger=f_zI_2$. Also $D_zP_z=0$ and $P_z$
acts as the identity on $\ker D_z$, so it is the orthogonal projection onto
that rank-two kernel. The connection $\nabla=P\,d$ is unitary. Differentiating
$D P=0$ and its adjoint, and using $D D^\dagger=fI_2$, gives
$$F_\nabla=P(dP\wedge dP)P =P\,dD^\dagger f^{-1}\wedge dD\,P.$$
Here the equality follows by writing $dP$ in the off-diagonal blocks for
$\mathbb C^4=\ker D\oplus\operatorname{im}D^\dagger$; each off-diagonal
block is respectively $-D^\dagger f^{-1}dD P$ and
$-P dD^\dagger f^{-1}D$, whose product inserts
$D D^\dagger=fI_2$.

In the coordinates of the Example,
$$dD= \begin{pmatrix} dz_2&-dz_1&0&0\\ -d\bar z_1&-d\bar z_2&0&0 \end{pmatrix}.$$
The only nonzero block of $dD^\dagger\wedge dD$ is its upper-left
$2\times2$ block:
$$\begin{pmatrix} -2i\theta_1&2(\theta_2-i\theta_3)\\ -2(\theta_2+i\theta_3)&2i\theta_1 \end{pmatrix},$$
where
$$\theta_1=dx^0\wedge dx^1-dx^2\wedge dx^3,\quad \theta_2=dx^0\wedge dx^2+dx^1\wedge dx^3,\quad \theta_3=dx^0\wedge dx^3-dx^1\wedge dx^2.$$
For the stated positive orientation, direct use of the Hodge-star definition
gives $*_g\theta_i=-\theta_i$ for each $i$. Every coefficient of
$dD^\dagger\wedge dD$ is therefore anti-self-dual. The scalar $f_z^{-1}$
and the degree-zero matrix factors $P_z$ in step 3.1 only take linear
combinations of these coefficient forms, so $*_gF_\nabla=-F_\nabla$ and
$F_\nabla^+=0$. No sign convention from a differently oriented stereographic
chart is used.

The residual $U(1)$ action sends
$I\mapsto gI$ and $J\mapsto Jg^{-1}$; it preserves the raw representative's
orbit, and its stabilizer is trivial because $gI=I$ with $I\ne0$ forces
$g=1$. The framed $W$ coordinates at infinity are fixed, so they introduce
no extra unitary factor. The finite monad resolution and [F3] give
$c_2(F)=H^2$, the unit charge under the positive incidence pullback
condition. The example verifies an exact one-instanton block with no
singularity because $f_z$ never vanishes.
